name: Magudeswarar Temple, Kodumudi (Thiruppandikodumudi)
deity: Shiva as Magudeswarar (Kodumudinathar), with the goddess Vadivudai Nayaki
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Kongu Nadu on the Kaveri, sung by Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar in the Tevaram (7th–8th century)
summary: On the west bank of the Kaveri, Kodumudi — the Thiruppandikodumudi of the Tevaram — honours Shiva as Magudeswarar, Lord of the summit, alongside shrines of Vishnu and Brahma in one sacred enclosure.

sections.history: Kodumudi is a river town of Erode district on the west bank of the Kaveri, and its temple is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams — a Paadal Petra Sthalam of Kongu Nadu that all three Tevaram saints sang. Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar each left a pathigam for the Lord of Thiruppandikodumudi, and Sundarar's is his celebrated hymn on the Namasivaya mantra, in which he vows that even should his mind forget the Lord, his tongue will go on saying the holy name. The old name itself joins the shrine to the Pandya kings, whose patronage the temple remembers, and it has been worshipped and enlarged by many generations since.
sections.architecture: The temple is known locally as a Trimurthy Kovil, for within one enclosure stand shrines to all three gods: Shiva as Magudeswarar, a small self-manifested lingam; Vishnu as Veeranarayana Perumal; and Brahma. The goddess Vadivudai Nayaki has her own shrine. Brahma here is shown with three faces rather than four, and the ancient vanni tree of the temple — its sthala vriksham, so old that no one can say its age — is revered as his fourth face. The bathing ghats of the Kaveri lie close by.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells of a contest between Adisesha, the serpent, and Vayu, the god of the wind, to settle which was the stronger. Adisesha coiled himself tightly around the peak of Mount Meru while Vayu blew with all his force. The peak shattered, and its fragments fell as gems in different places; the one that came to rest here became the self-manifested lingam. So the town is Kodumudi, the summit, and the Lord Magudeswarar — he who wears the crown of the mountain.
sections.festivals: The brahmotsavam is celebrated in Chithirai (April–May) as an eleven-day festival. Aadi Perukku in July–August draws the largest crowds, when devotees bathe at the Kaveri ghats and float lighted lamps on the river. Maha Shivaratri and Pradosham are also observed; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: A visit here is three darshans in one: Shiva, then Vishnu, then Brahma, each in his own shrine. Pause under the vanni tree, whose age is a mystery even to the temple, and walk down to the Kaveri ghats. The many Kaveri temples upstream and down make Kodumudi a natural halt on a Kongu Nadu pilgrimage.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most Kongu Nadu temples; hours are extended on festival days. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctums; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Kodumudi is about 40 km south-east of Erode by road, and has its own railway station on the Erode–Karur–Tiruchirappalli line. Erode and Karur are the nearest major junctions; Tiruchirappalli and Coimbatore airports are each a few hours away by road.
